passage: Dear Uma, I got home from the cricket ground last night and I am still thinking about the main gate. When the match ended, thousands tried to leave at once. A few young men pushed and shouted, and the whole crowd rocked like a boat. But most people just stood and waited, holding their children's hands and passing water bottles back to those behind. I made myself breathe slowly and noticed the two exits on the left, so I edged that way. Near the wall an old man was being squeezed, so a stranger and I made a small space and walked him to a steward. Nobody thanked us loudly, and that was fine. Write back soon. Irfan

qa.q: How many exits did Irfan notice on the left?
qa.a: Irfan noticed two exits on the left.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel while the crowd rocked, and what shows it?
qa.a: Irfan stayed calm on purpose; the slow breathing and the search for exits show a person keeping control.

qa.q: What could Irfan or others do next time before leaving a crowded gate?
qa.a: Spot the exits early, stay calm, and help anyone who is being squeezed reach a steward.

qa.q: What might the old man have felt against the wall, and then afterwards?
qa.a: Frightened while being squeezed, then relieved and safer once walked to a steward.

grounding: A visitor watches a crowd where a few push and most wait, and answers with calm, exits and helping a vulnerable person.

passage: Thanks for having me on the show, Farida. I'm Charu, and this was my first festival day in a temple town. The queue outside was enormous, and honestly I expected chaos. A few people slipped in from the side and there was some shoving near the barrier. But most folks just shuffled forward, sharing shade and water, and one volunteer kept calling, "Slowly, slowly, mind the little ones." I noticed the exit gate by the flower stalls and told myself to stay near it. When a grandmother nearly lost her footing, a teenager and I steadied her until a volunteer arrived. What stayed with me is how much of the crowd was quietly decent, and how little that showed on the news.

qa.q: What did one volunteer keep calling out?
qa.a: The volunteer kept calling, "Slowly, slowly, mind the little ones."

qa.q: What did Charu expect before joining the queue, and how did that expectation change?
qa.a: Charu expected chaos, but seeing most people share shade and water turned that fear into respect.

qa.q: What would you advise a first-time visitor to do in a festival queue?
qa.a: Notice the exit early, stay near it, keep calm and watch for anyone who might fall.

qa.q: What might the grandmother have felt when a teenager and Charu steadied her?
qa.a: Probably a jolt of fear at first, then gratitude and safety.

grounding: A visitor sees most people patient and a few causing chaos at a temple, and shows calm, an exit and help for a vulnerable person.

passage: The ball flew off Hrithik's bat and straight through the ground-floor window of the flat beside the community centre. Glass rattled onto the tiles. Hrithik ran behind the storeroom and crouched there, heart thumping. When Coach Maya came looking, Hrithik pointed and said, "Dilnaz hit it." Dilnaz's mouth fell open. The coach knelt down and asked quietly, "Are you sure? Tell me what you saw." Hrithik's eyes filled. "It was me." The coach phoned Hrithik's mother, who arrived in ten minutes. Together they knocked on the neighbour's door. "I broke your window and I lied about it. I'm sorry," Hrithik said in a small voice. Afterwards Hrithik walked over to Dilnaz and said sorry there too.

qa.q: Who did Hrithik blame for hitting the ball?
qa.a: Hrithik pointed and said Dilnaz hit it.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling behind the storeroom, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Fear; the thumping heart and crouching out of sight show Hrithik was scared of being found out.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than hiding, and why?
qa.a: Facing the neighbour with a parent and saying sorry, including to Dilnaz, put things right and ended the lie.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Hrithik pointed at them?
qa.a: Shocked and unfairly blamed; the open mouth shows surprise, and the later sorry probably brought some relief.

grounding: A child breaks a window, hides, blames another child, then faces the neighbour with a parent and apologises.

passage: The ball hit my kitchen window at about five, and the glass fell into the sink. From behind the curtain I saw Tarun drop the bat and dive behind the scooters. Then I heard, "Bhavya did it, not me!" Poor Bhavya just stood there with both hands up. I did not go out shouting. I wiped my hands and waited. Near dinner time there was a knock. Tarun stood at my door beside Tarun's father, who held a folded newspaper for the broken glass. Tarun looked at my slippers and said, "I broke it. I blamed Bhavya. Sorry." I cannot say what Tarun was feeling, but the shaky voice told me something. I said thank you for telling me. Damini

qa.q: Where did the ball land?
qa.a: The ball hit Damini's kitchen window.

qa.q: What might Tarun have been feeling at the door, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Nervous shame; looking at the slippers and the shaky voice suggest it, though Damini cannot be sure.

qa.q: What choice by Tarun mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Coming to the door with a parent to admit both the break and the blame, which repaired trust with Damini.

qa.q: How might Bhavya have felt when Tarun shouted the name?
qa.a: Shocked and unfairly accused; standing with both hands up shows helplessness.

grounding: An observing neighbour sees a child break a window, hide and blame another child, then come to the door with a parent to say sorry.

passage: So yesterday, Sumit, Mrs. Iyer from downstairs rang our bell during my drum-pad practice. Not even the real drums, just the pad with the rubber top! I stood there feeling my face go hot. Why me? The dog on the second floor barks all morning and nobody says anything. I said, "I'm not that loud," and Mum gave me a look. Then Mrs. Iyer explained that she rests every afternoon and the thumping comes right through her ceiling. It was the first time I thought about the ceiling. We settled on practice after five, a folded towel under the pad, and a knock on the door if it is still too much. Honestly I'm still a bit annoyed, but the towel works. Kunal

qa.q: What arrangement did Kunal and Mrs. Iyer settle on?
qa.a: They settled on practice after five, a folded towel under the pad, and a knock on the door if it is still too much.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel when the bell rang, and what shows it?
qa.a: Embarrassed and unfairly picked on; Kunal's face went hot and the thought Why me? followed.

qa.q: What could Kunal try if the towel does not help enough?
qa.a: Talk politely to Mrs. Iyer, as agreed, and change the time or the volume together.

qa.q: What is it like for Mrs. Iyer when the thumping comes through the ceiling?
qa.a: Tiring and irritating, because the afternoon rest is interrupted, so a polite request makes sense.

grounding: A teenager feels unfairly targeted by a noise complaint and reaches a compromise on time and volume.

passage: I'm Sudha, on the ground floor of B block, and I see everything from my window. The boys play cricket in the lane every evening at six. Yesterday the ball rattled Mr. Khanna's car door and he shouted from his balcony. Eshaan, the youngest bat, went quiet and stared at the ground. The others drifted off. I honestly can't tell if Eshaan was hurt or just cross. Later I saw Eshaan and Mr. Khanna talking at the gate, both speaking calmly. This morning I heard the deal: play until half past seven, keep the ball away from the parked cars, and use the wall end of the lane. Mr. Khanna even offered to hold the stumps once.

qa.q: What time do the boys play cricket in the lane?
qa.a: The boys play cricket in the lane every evening at six.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling after Mr. Khanna shouted, and how sure can Sudha be?
qa.a: Hurt and singled out, maybe also cross; Sudha saw silence and staring but says it is impossible to be sure.

qa.q: Which choice helped settle the dispute, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing a finish time, keeping the ball away from cars and using the wall end met the needs of both sides.

qa.q: Why might Mr. Khanna have reacted the way he did?
qa.a: The ball hit his car and the evening quiet, so he was worried and irritated, not just trying to spoil the game.

grounding: A teenager is shouted at over evening cricket, then a polite compromise on time and place settles the noise dispute.

passage:
Lalremsiami: Some guy parked in my slot AGAIN 😠
Sarika: Is the slot numbered?
Lalremsiami: Yes, 14, painted on the ground. I blocked his bike with mine.
Sarika: Hmm. And then?
Lalremsiami: If I move first, he wins. I'm not being the weak one.
Sarika: It's not about winning, no? Is he a resident?
Lalremsiami: Flat 302.
Sarika: Check the society rules?
Lalremsiami: Fine. Rules say numbered slots belong to the flat. I'll just say it politely.
Lalremsiami: Told him calmly. He said sorry, his own slot was being repaired, and moved the bike. We're good 🙂

qa.q: Which slot number is painted on the ground?
qa.a: Slot 14 is painted on the ground.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami block the bike instead of moving away?
qa.a: Because giving in felt like losing and being weak; the anger and pride show in the line If I move first, he wins.

qa.q: What small step calmed things down?
qa.a: Reading the society rules and speaking politely, instead of fighting over who wins.

qa.q: How might the neighbour from flat 302 have felt on finding the bike blocked?
qa.a: Annoyed or cornered at first, but the calm talk let the neighbour apologise and explain the repair instead of defending.

grounding: A young adult argues over a parking slot and feels giving in is weak, then settles it with calm talk and the society's rules.

passage: Yamini stubbed a toe on the water pots again. Vasudha Aunty from the first-floor flat left them on the shared stairway every evening, and the landing of the old kasba building was barely wide enough for two people. Yamini stomped upstairs already drafting a sharp speech. Giving way again would make everyone think Yamini was soft. On the wall by the door hung the landlord's faded notice: keep the stairs clear. Yamini took a breath, knocked and said, "Aunty, I tripped on the pots. Could we keep them by the railing? I'll help carry them up." Vasudha blinked, then laughed. "Beta, I never noticed. Yes, of course." The next evening the pots stood in a neat row.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha keep the water pots?
qa.a: Vasudha kept the water pots on the shared stairway.

qa.q: What was Yamini afraid that giving way would mean?
qa.a: Being seen as soft or weak, which fed the irritation and the sharp speech.

qa.q: What made Yamini's approach work?
qa.a: Calm words, a clear request and an offer to carry the pots let Vasudha agree without losing face.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt when Yamini knocked?
qa.a: Surprised at first, then relaxed and friendly, since Vasudha had not noticed the problem.

grounding: A young adult who feels giving in is weak settles a shared-stairway problem with calm, fair words.

passage: The residents' meeting in the laundry room of the Dublin block ran forty minutes before Nkechi understood how it worked: two neighbours, Mr. Doyle and Mrs. Kearney, spoke to each other while the rest looked at their shoes. Ingrid, from the top floor, opened her mouth twice and closed it again. Nkechi, twenty years old, had come only because the notice was under the door. Then Nkechi raised a hand. "Is there a written agenda? And are the bin rules written down anywhere?" A pause. Mr. Doyle said there had never been. "Could we make one, and could everyone say one thing they need?" Ingrid murmured, "Actually, the lift..." and the room turned to listen.

qa.q: Which two neighbours did most of the talking?
qa.a: Mr. Doyle and Mrs. Kearney spoke to each other.

qa.q: What did Nkechi realise about the meeting, and why speak up?
qa.a: Two neighbours were running everything while others stayed silent, so Nkechi wanted written rules and turns to speak so it could be fair.

qa.q: What could Nkechi do after this meeting to keep it fair?
qa.a: Help write the agenda and rules down and invite every resident to name one need.

qa.q: What might Ingrid have been feeling before the room turned to listen?
qa.a: Hesitant and unsure, wanting to speak about the lift but afraid to interrupt; opening and closing the mouth shows it.

grounding: A young resident notices a few people dominating a meeting and asks for written rules and turns to speak.

passage: Forty residents sat on plastic chairs in the society clubhouse, but only about four voices were heard. Gurpreet, a new tenant of twenty, watched the treasurer and a retired colonel argue about generator charges for half an hour. Jatin, from B wing, sat with folded arms, tapping a pen but never speaking. Nobody had seen the by-laws. At the end, Gurpreet went up to the secretary and asked, "Can I get a copy of the rules, please, and the last meeting's minutes?" Then, to the room, "Jatin, it looked like you had a point about parking?" Jatin blinked, then nodded. The secretary promised copies by Sunday, and next time the turns to speak would be written on the board.

qa.q: How many residents sat in the clubhouse?
qa.a: Forty residents sat on plastic chairs in the clubhouse.

qa.q: Why might Gurpreet have turned to ask Jatin directly?
qa.a: Gurpreet noticed the silent pen-tapping and wanted the quiet resident to have a chance to speak.

qa.q: Which request by Gurpreet helped the society work better for all?
qa.a: Asking for the rules and the minutes in writing, and for turns to speak on the board.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin sitting silent while others argue?
qa.a: Frustrating and unheard, with a point about parking but no obvious space to share it, until someone asks.

grounding: A young resident sees a few people dominate a society meeting and asks for written rules and fair turns.

passage: Sit, Abhinav, and I'll tell you about the year I moved to a colony in Nagpur. I was twenty-four, working late at the printing press and coming home at ten. By the second week I heard whispers at the water tap: where does she go so late, why no husband yet? My face burned. I wanted to snap back. Instead I began saying good evening to everyone, and when Mrs. Bhatt was struggling with her shopping, I carried a bag up the stairs. I told her plainly, "I work at the press till nine, and my marriage is my parents' and my own business for now." She said, "Oh." The whispers dried up like a puddle in May. It took two months, mind you. These days the whole colony calls me Vasudha Aunty.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha work when moving to the colony?
qa.a: Vasudha worked late at the printing press.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when hearing the whispers at the water tap?
qa.a: Hurt and angry; the burning face and the urge to snap back show it.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make instead of snapping back, and what did it change?
qa.a: Vasudha greeted everyone, helped Mrs. Bhatt and spoke plainly about work, and the whispers slowly dried up.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Bhatt have seen Vasudha after the bag and the plain words?
qa.a: As a helpful, honest neighbour rather than a mystery; the surprised Oh suggests a rethink.

grounding: A young person hears neighbours gossip about late hours and marriage and answers with a steady, polite, open manner.

passage: Rain had flooded two roads, so Aditi reached the colony gate at eleven, soaked, with Lakshmi from the office dropping her in an auto. A power cut had left the compound dark, and under the stairwell three neighbours stood around a candle, whispering. Aditi caught "always so late" and "who is this girl every night?" Her ears went warm. She wanted to hurry past. Instead she stopped and said, "Good evening, aunty. This is my colleague Lakshmi. The roads were flooded near the bus stand. Would you like my torch for the stairs?" One neighbour took it, looking embarrassed. Lakshmi grinned as they climbed. "That worked better than a fight, no?"

qa.q: Why did Aditi reach the gate at eleven?
qa.a: Rain had flooded two roads.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when overhearing the whispers?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stung; her ears went warm and she wanted to hurry past.

qa.q: Which choice turned the moment, and why?
qa.a: Stopping to explain openly and offering the torch showed nothing to hide and gave the gossip little to feed on.

qa.q: How might the neighbour who took the torch have felt?
qa.a: Embarrassed, maybe a little ashamed, and softened by the kindness.

grounding: A young person overhears neighbours discussing late hours and responds with a steady, polite and open manner.

passage: On the first morning of the new year, Yuki knocked on five doors of the Leeds block and left small plates of mochi, saying happy new year to each. Bilal, across the landing, returned the plate with samosas a week later. On a frosty morning Bilal's car would not start before an important appointment, and Yuki drove there without being asked. Months on, Yuki's Saturday music carried through the wall. Bilal sent a text: "Small request, could the bass go down a little tonight?" Yuki felt no sting, just a smile, and turned it down at once. Nobody needed a meeting or a letter. The greetings and plates had already made room for an easy word.

qa.q: What did Yuki leave on five doors at New Year?
qa.a: Yuki left small plates of mochi.

qa.q: What did Yuki feel on reading Bilal's text, and why?
qa.a: Relaxed and willing, because earlier kindness had built trust and the polite message did not feel like an attack.

qa.q: Why did the noise problem end so easily?
qa.a: Greetings, shared food and a lift had built goodwill, so both spoke kindly and the music went down.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt when Yuki drove on the frosty morning?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, which made it easier to ask politely later.

grounding: A young adult greets neighbours, shares festival food and helps in need, and goodwill makes a later conflict easy to settle.

passage: On Diwali evening the community centre hall smelled of ghee. Anjali set a tray of besan laddoos on the long table and said good evening to each person coming in, even the two who never nodded on the stairs. Tejas, from the flat opposite, took one and said, "I never thanked you for carrying my shopping last month." Anjali laughed. "You can thank me by joining the phone list for emergencies." Tejas wrote a name and number on the sign-up sheet. Weeks later, when the shared water tank overflowed at midnight, that list brought five neighbours in ten minutes, and a small squabble about whose turn it was to mop was over in a shrug.

qa.q: How long did it take five neighbours to arrive when the tank overflowed?
qa.a: Five neighbours arrived in ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Anjali greet even the two who never nodded, and what did Anjali want?
qa.a: To include everyone and build trust, hoping small warmth would open a connection.

qa.q: What small step by Anjali prepared the lane for the midnight overflow?
qa.a: Asking neighbours to join a phone list for emergencies.

qa.q: How does Tejas see Anjali?
qa.a: As a kind neighbour worth thanking; Tejas mentions the shopping and signs the list.

grounding: A young adult offers sweets and help to neighbours, and stored goodwill makes emergencies and small conflicts easier.

passage: A goat had nibbled the vegetable patch behind the tea stall, and Ramesh Kaka and Salma Bi were shouting across the fence. Pranav, home from the city for a week, leaned on a bicycle and watched. Within minutes a voice in the crowd said, "This is what happens with their lot," and another added a caste name. People began shuffling to two sides. Pranav felt his stomach tighten. He said, "It's about a goat and a patch, na? Let's not turn it into anything else." Then he walked to Master Hemant, the retired schoolteacher whom both families respected, and asked him to come. The teacher sat between the two, heard each in turn, and by evening the patch had a bamboo fence.

qa.q: What had the goat nibbled?
qa.a: A goat had nibbled the vegetable patch behind the tea stall.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when people began shuffling to two sides?
qa.a: Uneasy and worried; Pranav's stomach tightened at the labelling.

qa.q: What did Pranav do that stopped the quarrel from spreading?
qa.a: Pranav refused to join the labelling, kept it about the goat and patch, and asked the respected teacher to help.

qa.q: How might Salma Bi have felt when someone said their lot?
qa.a: Hurt and singled out, since a quarrel about a goat was turning into a judgement on who Salma Bi is.

grounding: An observer sees a small quarrel take on communal and caste colour and stops it by refusing labels and bringing in a neutral elder.

passage: Mrs. Ferreira and Mr. Haddad were arguing in the courtyard of the Lisbon block about a hosepipe left across the path. It began with two voices; soon there were four. "People like him never think of others," said a man from the second floor, and someone mentioned Mr. Haddad's mosque and where he came from. Siddiq, carrying groceries, stopped on the steps with a chill. "Sorry, but this is about a hose," Siddiq said. "Can we stay with the hose?" A few looked away. Later Siddiq knocked on Paulo's door. Paulo, the oldest tenant, was greeted warmly by both sides every morning. Paulo brought coffee to the courtyard table and asked each neighbour to tell it from the start.

qa.q: What was left across the path?
qa.a: A hosepipe was left across the path.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling on the steps when faith and origin entered the argument?
qa.a: Alarm and discomfort, like a chill, because a small quarrel was being turned into a judgement of who Mr. Haddad is.

qa.q: What could Siddiq or others do if the labelling starts again?
qa.a: Keep steering back to the hose, avoid repeating the labels, and ask a trusted neighbour such as Paulo to sit with both.

qa.q: How might Mr. Haddad feel when his mosque and origin were mentioned in a hose quarrel?
qa.a: Hurt and exposed, since a small dispute became a comment on who he is.

grounding: An observer sees a quarrel gain religious colour and refuses to join, cools it and brings in a neutral elder.

passage: I posted the trek photo at four. By five I had checked it eleven times, honestly I lost count. When it hit fifty likes I felt tall, like standing on a rooftop. Then nothing moved for an hour and my chest sank. Harsha, you know that feeling? At dinner my phone was under the table. Dad just said, "Are you enjoying that photo, or counting it?" No lecture. Then he added, "Fifty or five, you're still the one who climbed the hill." I didn't answer. Later I thought: I can't name ten of those fifty people. But the four friends who climbed with me didn't even click like, they sent me laughing voice notes. That was better than fifty. Sachin

qa.q: How many likes did the photo have when Sachin felt tall?
qa.a: The photo had fifty likes when Sachin felt tall.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when the likes stopped coming, and what shows it?
qa.a: Low and anxious; the chest sank and the phone went under the table at dinner.

qa.q: What could Sachin try next time after posting a photo?
qa.a: Put the phone away for a while and enjoy the trek with the friends who were there.

qa.q: How might Dad see Sachin's checking at dinner?
qa.a: With gentle concern; Dad asks whether Sachin is enjoying the photo or counting it, without lecturing.

grounding: A teenager feels proud at likes and low at silence, and a parent gently says numbers do not measure the person.

passage: I'm Mahima, and in our class Eshaan posts a short dance video every Friday. By second period the phone comes out under the desk. I sit right behind, so I see the screen. Last week it had two hundred likes by lunch and Eshaan was practically bouncing, showing everyone. This Friday the number stuck at thirty. Eshaan went quiet, refreshed again and again, and snapped at me for asking about homework. I honestly don't know if it was about the video. At break our teacher sat beside Eshaan and said, "Your video made me smile. Thirty or three hundred, it isn't a score for you." Eshaan shrugged, but I saw a small nod.

qa.q: How many likes did the video have by lunch last week?
qa.a: The video had two hundred likes by lunch last week.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling when the number stuck at thirty, and how sure can Mahima be?
qa.a: Disappointed and low, judging by the quiet and repeated refreshing, but Mahima does not know whether it was about the video.

qa.q: What could a friend add to what the teacher said?
qa.a: Invite Eshaan to talk or dance together offline, showing that the friendship does not depend on numbers.

qa.q: Why might the teacher have sat beside Eshaan at break?
qa.a: To speak gently and privately, without embarrassing Eshaan in front of others, and to show the number is not a score.

grounding: A teenager who posts and refreshes feels proud at likes and low at silence, and an adult gently says numbers are not a measure of a person.

passage: Come, sit, Tanuja. Sabina Aunty will tell you about the terrace. I was fifteen, and the whole class was recording a dance on the school terrace parapet. Everyone was cheering. I climbed up because saying no felt scarier than the drop. My knees shook and my smile was painted on. Down below, Roopa stayed on the floor and said, "No thanks, it's not for me. I'll hold your bag." And nobody stopped talking to Roopa. Nobody even blinked. I looked at her calm face and then at the edge, and I climbed down. That evening Roopa and I shared a packet of chips on the stairs like always, and the video went ahead without me.

qa.q: Where did the students record the dance?
qa.a: They recorded the dance on the school terrace parapet.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling on the parapet with shaking knees?
qa.a: Frightened but wanting to belong; the cheering pulled Sabina up while the shaking knees showed fear.

qa.q: What choice did Sabina make after seeing Roopa's refusal?
qa.a: Sabina climbed down from the parapet, seeing that Roopa's calm no cost no friendships.

qa.q: How might Roopa have felt saying no thanks in front of the class?
qa.a: Probably nervous but steady; offering to hold the bag shows a kind, friendly way to refuse.

grounding: A teenager joins a risky viral dance to fit in until a friend says no thanks and stays friends.

passage: Ten minutes before the school bus, the group crowded around the fountain in the courtyard. The challenge was to balance on the wet stone rim while a friend filmed. Everyone else had done it already. "Your turn, Kalyani, come on!" Kalyani's stomach flipped, but stepping up felt easier than being the only one who didn't. The rim was slick with morning rain and one foot slid. Francis caught Kalyani's sleeve. "You're fine. Honestly, I'm skipping mine, I'll film instead. No offence!" "None taken," someone laughed, and the filming went on. Kalyani stepped down, heart racing, and noticed nobody thought less of Francis. The bus horn sounded and they ran to it together.

qa.q: What was the rim of the fountain slick with?
qa.a: The rim was slick with morning rain.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani step up onto the rim even though the stomach flipped?
qa.a: Kalyani wanted to belong and feared being the only one who didn't; that outweighed the fear of slipping.

qa.q: What small step could Kalyani take next time?
qa.a: Say no thanks lightly like Francis and offer another role, such as filming.

qa.q: How do the others see Francis's choice to film instead?
qa.a: They accept it easily, laughing none taken, and Francis stays part of the group without doing the challenge.

grounding: A teenager joins a risky challenge to fit in, and a friend who says no thanks and stays friends shows other options.
